statement: In adults who regularly consumed a lot of caffeine and had minor surgery under general anaesthesia, caffeine tablets given around the time of surgery, compared with identical placebo tablets, reduced headache after surgery from 10 of 20 to 0 of 20 on the evening of surgery and from 7 of 20 to 1 of 20 the next morning, in one double-blind randomized trial (Hampl et al., 1995); gastric fluid volume and acidity, measured because caffeine stimulates stomach acid, did not differ significantly. The trial did not measure the effects on craving, fasting or costs that its authors suggest, was too small to judge safety, and excluded smokers and people with frequent headaches. Certainty: low. Status: single study.
plain: In one small hospital trial, caffeine tablets around surgery prevented most headaches in people who usually had a lot of caffeine.
population: 40 adults (27 women) who regularly consumed a lot of caffeine, non-smokers without frequent headaches, having minor elective surgery under general anaesthesia
exposure: Caffeine tablets given by hospital staff around the time of surgery (study amounts and timing on the study card)
comparator: Identical placebo tablets on the same schedule
outcome: Postoperative headache (yes or no) and other symptoms; gastric fluid volume and pH at surgery
magnitude: Headache 0 of 20 (caffeine) against 10 of 20 (placebo) on the evening of surgery, P < 0.001; 1 of 20 against 7 of 20 the next morning, P < 0.05; editors' calculation: risk differences 50 (95% CI 24 to 70) and 30 (5 to 52) percentage points. Gastric fluid volume 19.2 (SD 14.6) against 22.7 (SD 11.9) ml and pH 2.12 against 1.91, not significant.

evidence.extracted: Headache 0 of 20 with caffeine against 10 of 20 with placebo on the evening of surgery (P < 0.001) and 1 of 20 against 7 of 20 the next morning (P < 0.05); editors' calculation: risk differences 50 (95% CI 24 to 70) and 30 (5 to 52) percentage points.

risk_of_bias.note: Sequence generation and attrition not reported, no protocol, reporting errors (card overall: some concerns).

indirectness.note: Population, setting and treatment match the claim.

imprecision.note: 40 patients; safety outcomes far too few to judge; the next-morning difference is fragile.

grade.reasoning: A randomized double-blind trial starts high; downgraded for risk of bias and imprecision, giving low. Shares its single trial with the claim on caffeine-withdrawal headache (section 8); not independent evidence.
